entry_json.definition: to change something into a different form, or to change it so that it can be used for a different purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The old cotton mill has been converted into student flats.
example_sentences: Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity.
You can convert the figures into percentages to make the comparison clearer.

contexts.text: The old cotton mill has been converted into student flats.
Wind turbines convert the movement of air into usable power.
Governments should convert unused office blocks into affordable housing.

confusables.difference: Change is the neutral word for any difference. Convert means changing form or purpose deliberately, usually into something specific: you convert a garage into a bedroom, you do not convert your mind.
Transform is bigger and more dramatic, and often has no stated end product. Convert almost always names what it becomes, with into.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say "convert to flats" when you mean the building becomes flats. The normal pattern is convert something into something.

entry_json.definition: to make somebody believe that something is true, or to persuade them to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a week to convince my parents that studying abroad was worth the cost.
example_sentences: The evidence convinced the committee that the policy needed changing.
My friend convinced me to join the gym with her.

contexts.text: It took me a week to convince my parents that studying abroad was worth the cost.
These figures alone are unlikely to convince readers that the scheme has worked.

confusables.difference: Persuade is about getting somebody to act. Convince is about getting them to believe. You persuade a friend to come out; you convince a friend that the film is good.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write "convince about". Use convince somebody of something, or convince somebody that.

entry_json.definition: completely sure that something is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am convinced that online learning suits some students far better than lectures do.
example_sentences: She was convinced of his honesty long before the evidence appeared.
Not everyone is convinced that the new bypass will reduce traffic.

contexts.text: I am convinced that online learning suits some students far better than lectures do.
Honestly, I am not convinced by that argument at all.

confusables.difference: Convinced describes the person who now believes. Convincing describes the thing that made them believe. A convincing argument leaves you convinced.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the two -ed and -ing forms: "I am convincing" means you persuade others, not that you believe.

entry_json.definition: the most important or central part of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the core of the problem is a shortage of affordable housing, not a shortage of land.
example_sentences: Maths and language form the core of the primary curriculum.
The report goes to the core of why young people leave rural areas.

contexts.text: At the core of the problem is a shortage of affordable housing, not a shortage of land.
The core modules are compulsory, but you choose the rest yourself.

confusables.difference: Centre is usually physical position. Core is importance: the core of an argument is its essential part, not its middle.
Heart of the matter is warmer and more idiomatic; core is the drier, more academic choice for essays.

entry_json.avoid: In an essay, avoid "the core reason" when you simply mean the main reason; core works best as a noun in at the core of.

entry_json.definition: connected with a large company or with companies in general
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Corporate donations now fund a large share of university research.
example_sentences: Many graduates are drawn to corporate life by the salary rather than the work.
The company publishes an annual report on its corporate responsibility.

contexts.text: Corporate donations now fund a large share of university research.
I did not enjoy the corporate world, so I moved to a small charity.

confusables.difference: Commercial means done for profit or connected with buying and selling. Corporate means belonging to companies as organisations, so corporate culture is about how a firm behaves internally.

entry_json.avoid: Corporate describes companies, not individual businesspeople; a person is a business executive, not a corporate.

entry_json.definition: a set of clothes worn by an actor or performer, or the traditional clothes of a place or period
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the spring festival everyone wears traditional costume and dances in the square.
example_sentences: The museum has a room of nineteenth-century costume.
She spent a fortnight making her son's costume for the school play.

contexts.text: At the spring festival everyone wears traditional costume and dances in the square.
The exhibition traces changes in working-class costume between 1850 and 1900.

confusables.difference: Clothes is what you wear every day. Costume is worn for a performance, a festival or a period, so "I bought new costume" is wrong for ordinary shopping.
An outfit is a set of ordinary clothes chosen to go together; a costume represents a character, a country or a tradition.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use costume for daily clothing. In British English a swimming costume is a swimsuit, not fancy dress.

entry_json.definition: a small, usually old house in the countryside or in a village
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We rented a stone cottage in the hills for a week with no internet at all.
example_sentences: Her grandparents live in a cottage with a garden full of vegetables.
Holiday cottages have pushed local house prices beyond what young families can pay.

contexts.text: We rented a stone cottage in the hills for a week with no internet at all.
Second-home buyers have converted many village cottages into holiday lets.

confusables.difference: A bungalow is any house on one floor, town or country, new or old. A cottage is small, rural and usually old, and may well have stairs.

entry_json.avoid: A cottage is not a general word for house; a modern flat or a city house is never a cottage.

entry_json.definition: a soft white material from the cotton plant, used to make cloth and thread
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cotton production uses far more water than most shoppers realise.
example_sentences: I prefer cotton shirts because they are cooler in summer.
The country's economy still depends heavily on exports of raw cotton.

contexts.text: I prefer cotton shirts because they are cooler in summer.
Cotton production uses far more water than most shoppers realise.

confusables.difference: Cotton comes from a plant; wool comes from sheep. Both are uncountable when you mean the material.

entry_json.avoid: Cotton is uncountable as a material: say "a cotton shirt" or "some cotton", not "a cotton".

entry_json.definition: a group of people elected to govern a town or area, or a group chosen to advise or make decisions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The local council has closed two libraries to balance its budget.
example_sentences: Residents wrote to the council about the state of the pavements.
The student council meets once a month to discuss campus issues.

contexts.text: The local council has closed two libraries to balance its budget.
I rang the council about the bins and they came the next day.

confusables.difference: Counsel with an s is advice, or a lawyer. Council with a c is the body of people. They sound the same, so the spelling is the only signal in writing.
Government usually means the national one. Council is local: it runs schools, roads and rubbish collection in one town or district.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write counsel when you mean the elected body; the spelling error is common and costs marks in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: land outside towns and cities, with fields, farms and woods
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Young people keep leaving the countryside because the jobs are all in the cities.
example_sentences: At weekends we drive out into the countryside to walk.
Protecting the countryside from new housing is a constant political argument.

contexts.text: At weekends we drive out into the countryside to walk.
Young people keep leaving the countryside because the jobs are all in the cities.

confusables.difference: Nature is the natural world in general, including wild places. Countryside is farmed, settled land outside cities, and it is uncountable and normally takes the.
Country can mean a nation. The countryside never does: "I live in the countryside" means rural area, "I live in this country" means the nation.

entry_json.avoid: Countryside is uncountable and normally takes the: not "a countryside" or "countrysides".

entry_json.definition: one of the areas that a country such as Britain or the United States is divided into for local government
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Funding for schools varies sharply from one county to another.
example_sentences: She grew up in a small village in a rural county in the north.
The county council is responsible for maintaining these roads.

contexts.text: Funding for schools varies sharply from one county to another.
My family has lived in the same county for four generations.

confusables.difference: A country is a nation. A county is an administrative area inside one. One letter changes the meaning completely, and examiners notice.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use county for a nation state; that is country.

entry_json.definition: the ability to do something dangerous or difficult even though you are afraid
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It takes real courage to move to a country where you know nobody.
example_sentences: She never found the courage to tell her manager she was leaving.
The rescue team showed extraordinary courage during the floods.
collocations: have the courage to do something

contexts.text: It takes real courage to move to a country where you know nobody.
Reform of this kind requires political courage rather than new funding.

confusables.difference: Confidence is believing you can do it. Courage is doing it although you are afraid. A shy person can act with courage without confidence.
Brave is the adjective for the person; courage is the noun for the quality. Say "she was brave" or "she showed courage", never "she was courage".

entry_json.avoid: Courage is uncountable: not "a courage" or "courages".

entry_json.definition: a place where legal cases are decided by a judge, or a marked area where a sport such as tennis is played
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The case went to court and took two years to settle.
example_sentences: There are four tennis courts behind the sports centre.
The company was taken to court over the way it disposed of waste.

contexts.text: The case went to court and took two years to settle.
We book a court on Sunday mornings when it is cheaper.

confusables.difference: In British English football and cricket are played on a pitch; tennis, basketball and badminton on a court.
The court is the institution or the room; the trial is the process that happens in it.

entry_json.avoid: In the legal sense, the fixed phrases drop the article: go to court, appear in court, not "go to the court".

entry_json.definition: having something over or on the surface, or having a roof
entry_json.own_context_sentence: By March the fields were still covered with snow.
example_sentences: The market is covered, so it stays open in bad weather.
After an hour of cycling my jacket was covered in dust.

contexts.text: By March the fields were still covered with snow.
My desk is covered in books at the moment because of the exams.

confusables.difference: Full of means the inside is filled. Covered in means the outside has a layer on it: a bag full of sand, a table covered in sand.

entry_json.avoid: Use covered in or covered with, not "covered by", when you mean a layer on a surface.

entry_json.definition: an accident in which a vehicle hits something violently; also a sudden serious fall in prices or a computer failure
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Lower speed limits have cut the number of serious crashes on rural roads.
example_sentences: Nobody was badly hurt in the crash, but both cars were written off.
The 2008 financial crash changed how young people think about mortgages.

contexts.text: Lower speed limits have cut the number of serious crashes on rural roads.
The traffic was terrible because there had been a crash on the ring road.

confusables.difference: Accident covers anything unintended, including cutting your finger. A crash involves a vehicle hitting something, so it is narrower and more violent.
Collision is the formal, technical word used in reports; crash is normal in both speech and journalism.

entry_json.avoid: For computers say "my laptop crashed", not "my laptop had a crash" in speech, though the noun is fine in technical writing.

entry_json.definition: the act of making something that did not exist before
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The creation of new cycle lanes has made the city centre noticeably quieter.
example_sentences: The main benefit of the scheme is the creation of skilled jobs.
Job creation in the region has slowed since the factory closed.

contexts.text: The creation of new cycle lanes has made the city centre noticeably quieter.
What the town really needs is job creation, not more shopping centres.

confusables.difference: Creativity is the ability to have original ideas. Creation is the act or the thing made. A student shows creativity; a government funds the creation of jobs.

entry_json.avoid: In an essay, "the creation of X" is a useful nominalisation, but do not stack it: "the creation of the development of X" is unreadable.

entry_json.definition: a living thing, especially an animal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Deep-sea creatures are still poorly understood because the habitat is so hard to reach.
example_sentences: Bats are shy creatures and rarely come near people.
Farming chemicals harm many of the small creatures that live in the soil.

contexts.text: Deep-sea creatures are still poorly understood because the habitat is so hard to reach.
I love watching the little creatures in the pond at my grandmother's house.

confusables.difference: Animal is the plain scientific word. Creature is slightly warmer or vaguer, and is used when the exact species does not matter, or for imaginary beings.

entry_json.avoid: Creature is countable; do not use it for plants, and avoid it in strictly scientific writing where animal or organism is expected.

entry_json.definition: all the people working on a ship, an aircraft or a film, or a team doing a particular job
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cabin crew handled the delay calmly, which made a long wait bearable.
example_sentences: A crew of six maintains the lighthouse throughout the winter.
The film crew spent three weeks filming in the mountains.

contexts.text: The cabin crew handled the delay calmly, which made a long wait bearable.
Ships now sail with smaller crews because so much is automated.

confusables.difference: Staff is the general word for people employed anywhere. Crew is for a vehicle or a specific operation: hotel staff, but cabin crew.
The crew work on the vehicle; the passengers are carried by it.

entry_json.avoid: Crew is a group noun: say "a member of the crew" or "three crew members", not "three crews" when you mean three people.

entry_json.definition: a time of great difficulty or danger when important decisions must be made
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The housing crisis in large cities has pushed young workers ever further from the centre.
example_sentences: The hospital was struggling long before the crisis began.
Governments tend to act on climate change only when it becomes a visible crisis.

contexts.text: The housing crisis in large cities has pushed young workers ever further from the centre.
It felt like a crisis at the time, but we sorted it out in the end.

confusables.difference: A problem is anything that needs solving, large or small. A crisis is severe, urgent and usually affects many people, so do not call a late bus a crisis.
An emergency is sudden and demands action in minutes or hours; a crisis can last for years.

entry_json.avoid: The plural is crises, pronounced ˈkraɪsiːz, not "crisises".

entry_json.definition: a person who expresses disapproval of somebody or something, or who writes judgements about art, films or books
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Critics of the policy argue that it helps landlords rather than tenants.
example_sentences: The film was praised by critics but ignored by audiences.
Even his fiercest critics admit that he improved the transport system.

contexts.text: Critics of the policy argue that it helps landlords rather than tenants.
I never read the critics before I watch a film; I would rather decide myself.

confusables.difference: A critic is the person; criticism is what they produce. "He received a lot of critics" is a very common error for "a lot of criticism".
Critical is the adjective, and it also means extremely important, so context decides which sense is meant.

entry_json.avoid: Never use critics as an uncountable noun meaning disapproval; that word is criticism.

entry_json.definition: expressing disapproval; or extremely important because a situation depends on it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The next ten years will be critical if emissions are to be reduced in time.
example_sentences: The report is highly critical of the way the money was spent.
Students need to develop critical thinking rather than memorise answers.

contexts.text: The next ten years will be critical if emissions are to be reduced in time.
My tutor was quite critical of my first draft, but she was right.

confusables.difference: Crucial only means decisively important. Critical carries both that sense and the sense of finding fault, so context has to make it clear.
Being critical of something can be constructive analysis; criticising usually just means attacking it.

entry_json.avoid: Use critical of, not "critical to", when you mean disapproving; critical to means essential for.

entry_json.definition: the act of saying what you think is wrong with somebody or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main criticism of the scheme is that it was designed without asking residents.
example_sentences: She takes criticism well and usually acts on it.
The proposal has attracted criticism from both sides of the debate.

contexts.text: The main criticism of the scheme is that it was designed without asking residents.
I do not mind criticism as long as it is constructive.

confusables.difference: Criticism is the comment; a critic is the person making it. "There were many criticisms" is right; "there were many critics" means many people, not many comments.
Feedback is neutral and can be positive; criticism is negative unless you add constructive.

entry_json.avoid: Criticism is normally uncountable, so prefer "a lot of criticism"; use criticisms only for separate specific points.

entry_json.definition: to say what you think is wrong or bad about somebody or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The government has been criticized for cutting funding without consulting schools.
example_sentences: It is easy to criticize a plan without offering a better one.
She criticized the report for relying on out-of-date figures.

contexts.text: The government has been criticized for cutting funding without consulting schools.
My parents never criticized my choice of subject, which helped a lot.

confusables.difference: You criticize an action or an idea; you blame a person for a result. "They blamed the driver" and "they criticized the decision" are not interchangeable.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is criticize somebody for doing something, not "criticize somebody about". Both spellings criticize and criticise are accepted; keep one throughout.

entry_json.definition: a plant grown by farmers for food or sale, or the amount of it gathered in one season
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two dry summers in a row have ruined the region's main crop.
example_sentences: Rice remains the most important crop in much of Asia.
Farmers rotate crops so that the soil does not lose its nutrients.

contexts.text: Two dry summers in a row have ruined the region's main crop.
My grandfather still grows a few crops on the land behind the house.

confusables.difference: The crop is what grows; the harvest is the act of gathering it, or the total gathered. You plant a crop and then bring in the harvest.
Any plant can be a plant; only one grown deliberately for food or profit is a crop.

entry_json.avoid: Crop is countable: say "crops are grown", not "crop is grown", when you mean farming in general.

entry_json.definition: extremely important because everything else depends on it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Early education is crucial in deciding how well children do later on.
example_sentences: Access to clean water is crucial for public health.
The first month of a new job is crucial for building relationships.

contexts.text: Early education is crucial in deciding how well children do later on.
Sleep is crucial for me; without it I cannot concentrate at all.

confusables.difference: Crucial is the strong end of important: it means the outcome depends on it. Using crucial for every point in an essay drains it of force.
Essential means it cannot be left out. Crucial means it decides the result. Water is essential to life; timing is crucial to success.

entry_json.avoid: Crucial is already an extreme adjective, so avoid "very crucial"; use absolutely crucial if you need emphasis.

entry_json.definition: deliberately causing pain or suffering to people or animals, and not caring about it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many people now regard keeping large animals in small enclosures as cruel.
example_sentences: It would be cruel to leave a dog alone all day.
Children can be surprisingly cruel to anyone who seems different.

contexts.text: Many people now regard keeping large animals in small enclosures as cruel.
I think it is cruel to buy a puppy and then leave it alone all day.

confusables.difference: Unkind is mild and usually about words or manner. Cruel implies real suffering and an intention to cause it.
Violent describes physical force. Cruelty can be entirely verbal or consist of neglect.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is cruel to somebody, not "cruel with somebody". The noun is cruelty, not "cruelness".

entry_json.definition: connected with the customs, beliefs and arts of a society
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living abroad taught me that most misunderstandings are cultural rather than linguistic.
example_sentences: The city has a rich cultural life for a place of its size.
Cultural differences in how directly people speak can cause friction at work.

contexts.text: Cultural differences in how directly people speak can cause friction at work.
Living abroad taught me that most misunderstandings are cultural rather than linguistic.

confusables.difference: Traditional means handed down from the past. Cultural covers anything belonging to a society's way of life, including modern art and current habits.

entry_json.avoid: Cultural is an adjective only; the noun is culture. Not "the cultural of my country".

entry_json.definition: a medicine or treatment that makes an illness go away; also a solution to a problem
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is still no cure for the common cold, only ways of easing it.
example_sentences: Researchers have spent decades searching for a cure for this disease.
Cheap loans are no cure for an economy that produces nothing.

contexts.text: Researchers have spent decades searching for a cure for this disease.
My grandmother swears that honey and lemon is a cure for everything.

confusables.difference: Treatment manages an illness and may continue for years; a cure ends it. Diabetes has treatments but no cure.
Medicine is the substance you take; a cure is the result it achieves.

entry_json.avoid: Use cure for, not "cure of", when naming the illness.

entry_json.definition: the system of money that a country uses
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A weak currency makes imported food more expensive for ordinary families.
example_sentences: I changed some currency at the airport, though the rate was poor.
Several countries share a single currency, which limits what each can do alone.

contexts.text: A weak currency makes imported food more expensive for ordinary families.
I always take a little local currency with me in case cards are not accepted.

confusables.difference: Money is the general uncountable idea. A currency is a particular national system, so you can count currencies but not moneys.
Cash means notes and coins rather than cards; currency means the system, whatever form it takes.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use currency to mean the amount you have: "I have no currency" should be "I have no money".

entry_json.definition: happening or existing now
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The current system rewards students who memorise rather than those who think.
example_sentences: My current job is temporary, but I am hoping it becomes permanent.
Under current rules, applicants must live in the district for a year.

contexts.text: The current system rewards students who memorise rather than those who think.
My current job is temporary, but I am hoping it becomes permanent.

confusables.difference: In English, actual means real, not present. If you mean now, use current: "my current address", not "my actual address".
Present and current are close, but present is more formal and normally sits before the noun: the present government, the current government.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use current to mean common or usual; that is a false friend from several European languages.

entry_json.definition: at the present time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library is currently closed for refurbishment, so we study in the café.
example_sentences: About a third of the workforce is currently employed part time.
I am currently in my second year of an engineering degree.

contexts.text: About a third of the workforce is currently employed part time.
I am currently in my second year of an engineering degree.

confusables.difference: Recently points at the near past and often takes the present perfect. Currently points at now and takes the present simple or continuous.
In British English presently often means soon, so currently is the safer word for now.

entry_json.avoid: Currently belongs with present tenses. "I currently worked there" is wrong; use "I currently work there".

entry_json.definition: a piece of cloth hung to cover a window, or the large cloth in front of a theatre stage
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thick curtains keep the heat in, which cuts our energy bill in winter.
example_sentences: She drew the curtains and switched on the lamp.
The curtain rose and the hall went silent.

contexts.text: Thick curtains keep the heat in, which cuts our energy bill in winter.
Simple measures such as fitting heavy curtains reduce household heat loss.

confusables.difference: A blind is a stiff sheet that rolls or folds up; a curtain is soft cloth that you pull sideways.

entry_json.avoid: Draw the curtains can mean either open or close them, so add a word if it matters: draw the curtains back.

entry_json.definition: a line that bends smoothly, with no sharp angles
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The curve on the graph rises steeply after 2010 and then levels off.
example_sentences: There is a sharp curve in the road just before the village.
The learning curve was steep, but after a month the software felt natural.

contexts.text: The curve on the graph rises steeply after 2010 and then levels off.
The learning curve was steep, but after a month the software felt natural.

confusables.difference: In Task 1 writing, line is the neutral word for any plotted series; curve suggests it bends rather than running straight.
A bend is usually in a road or river and can be sharp; a curve is smooth and works for graphs and shapes too.

entry_json.avoid: In Academic Task 1, describe the trend rather than the shape: "sales rose sharply" reads better than "the curve went up".

entry_json.definition: having the shape of a curve; bent in a smooth line
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new terminal has a curved glass roof that floods the hall with light.
example_sentences: A curved screen is said to be easier on the eyes.
The path is gently curved so that cyclists slow down naturally.

contexts.text: The new terminal has a curved glass roof that floods the hall with light.
I like the curved design of the new bridge more than the old flat one.

confusables.difference: Round means circular or spherical overall. Curved only says that a line or surface bends; a curved wall is not round.
Bent often implies damage or force applied. Curved is neutral and usually deliberate design.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use curved for a person's posture; that is stooped or hunched.

entry_json.definition: an accepted way of behaving that has existed among a group of people for a long time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is a custom in my country to take fruit when you visit somebody's home.
example_sentences: Local customs vary enormously even within one region.
The custom of eating together on Fridays has survived in many families.

contexts.text: It is a custom in my country to take fruit when you visit somebody's home.
Migration has weakened some customs while creating new ones.

confusables.difference: A habit belongs to one person and may be trivial. A custom belongs to a whole community and has lasted for generations.
Tradition is grander and often ceremonial; a custom can be an everyday courtesy such as removing your shoes.

entry_json.avoid: Customs in the plural also means the airport check on goods, so make the meaning clear from context.

entry_json.definition: physical harm caused to something, making it less useful or valuable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The storm caused serious damage to homes along the coast.
example_sentences: Plastic waste does lasting damage to marine life.
The flat had some water damage, which is why the rent was low.

contexts.text: Plastic waste does lasting damage to marine life.
The flat had some water damage, which is why the rent was low.

confusables.difference: Harm covers injury to people, health and interests. Damage is mainly physical and applies to objects, buildings and the environment.
People suffer injuries; things suffer damage. "He had serious damage" is wrong for a person.

entry_json.avoid: Damage is uncountable in this sense: say "a lot of damage", not "many damages". Damages in the plural means money paid in a court case.

entry_json.definition: a formal or public discussion in which people put opposing views
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is an ongoing debate about whether homework benefits younger children.
example_sentences: The debate over road pricing has divided the city for years.
Our class held a debate on whether zoos should be closed.

contexts.text: There is an ongoing debate about whether homework benefits younger children.
Our class held a debate on whether zoos should be closed.

confusables.difference: A discussion can be friendly and open-ended. A debate has sides, and each side argues for a position.
An argument is often personal and angry, or it means a single reason. A debate is organised and public.

entry_json.avoid: Use debate about or debate over. As a verb, debate takes a direct object: "they debated the issue", not "they debated about the issue".

entry_json.definition: a period of ten years
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Over the past decade, car ownership in the city has fallen by a fifth.
example_sentences: The technology has changed beyond recognition in two decades.
She has taught at the same school for more than a decade.

contexts.text: Over the past decade, car ownership in the city has fallen by a fifth.
She has taught at the same school for more than a decade.

confusables.difference: A decade is ten years; a century is a hundred. Learners often reach for century when the data covers only a few years.

entry_json.avoid: Note the stress: DEC-ade, not de-CADE. "In the last decade" pairs with the present perfect, not the past simple.

entry_json.definition: of an acceptable or reasonably good standard; or honest and fair towards other people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everyone deserves decent housing and a decent wage, whatever job they do.
example_sentences: The hotel was nothing special, but the breakfast was decent.
He is a decent man who would never take advantage of anyone.

contexts.text: Everyone deserves decent housing and a decent wage, whatever job they do.
The hotel was nothing special, but the breakfast was decent.

confusables.difference: Good is a straightforward compliment. Decent means good enough rather than impressive, so calling an essay decent is faint praise.
Adequate is colder and more formal; decent carries a note of approval and is common in speech.

entry_json.avoid: In the sense of good enough, decent is informal. In Task 2, prefer adequate or reasonable; keep decent for decent wages and decent housing, which are fixed collocations.

entry_json.definition: to say something officially or publicly; or to tell the authorities about income or goods
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several councils have declared a climate emergency without changing their spending.
example_sentences: The region was declared a national park in 1951.
Travellers must declare any goods worth more than the duty-free limit.

contexts.text: The region was declared a national park in 1951.
At the airport you have to declare anything you are bringing in to sell.

confusables.difference: Announce is telling people news. Declare is more formal and more official, and it often creates the new state of affairs: declaring war starts it.
State simply means say clearly. Declare adds authority or public formality.

entry_json.avoid: Declare is too formal for ordinary conversation; "he declared he was tired" sounds odd where said would do.

entry_json.definition: a continuous fall in the amount, quality or importance of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart shows a steady decline in newspaper sales between 2000 and 2020.
example_sentences: There has been a sharp decline in the number of bees in recent years.
The industry went into decline once the mines closed.

contexts.text: The chart shows a steady decline in newspaper sales between 2000 and 2020.
The high street in my town has been in decline since the big shops left.

confusables.difference: Decrease is neutral and purely numerical. Decline suggests a worsening as well as a fall, so it fits sales, health and standards better than it fits temperature.
As a verb, decline also means politely refuse. "She declined the offer" has nothing to do with falling numbers.

entry_json.avoid: Use a decline in something, not "a decline of something", when naming what fell.

entry_json.definition: to make something look more attractive by adding things to it; in British English, also to paint or paper a room
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We spent the weekend decorating the spare room before my sister arrived.
example_sentences: The whole street is decorated with lights during the festival.
She decorated the cake with fruit rather than icing.

contexts.text: We spent the weekend decorating the spare room before my sister arrived.
Public buildings are decorated with flags for the national holiday.

confusables.difference: Design is planning how something will look or work before it is made. Decorate is adding attractive detail to something that already exists.

entry_json.avoid: In British English, decorating a room usually means painting it, not adding ornaments, so add with lights or with flowers if that is your meaning.

entry_json.definition: something added to make a thing look more attractive, or the act of adding it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The decorations stay up until the first week of January.
example_sentences: The building is plain outside, with all the decoration inside.
We made most of the decorations ourselves out of paper.

contexts.text: We made most of the decorations ourselves out of paper.
The building is plain outside, with all the decoration inside.

confusables.difference: An ornament is a single object kept for display. Decoration can be uncountable and covers patterns and finishes as well as objects.

entry_json.avoid: Countable decorations means the individual items; uncountable decoration means the style or the work. Choose deliberately.

entry_json.definition: to become smaller in size, number or amount, or to make something smaller
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Water use decreased sharply after meters were installed.
example_sentences: The number of road deaths has decreased steadily since the 1990s.
Cycling to work decreases both costs and stress.

contexts.text: Water use decreased sharply after meters were installed.
My screen time has decreased a lot since I started running.

confusables.difference: Reduce needs somebody or something to do it: you reduce prices. Decrease can happen by itself: prices decreased. Both work as transitive verbs, but decrease is the safer intransitive one.
Fall is shorter and more natural in speech; decrease is the formal Task 1 word.

entry_json.avoid: Note the stress shift: the verb is dɪˈkriːs, the noun ˈdiːkriːs. Use decrease by for the size of the change and decrease to for the end point.

entry_json.definition: very strongly or intensely, especially about feelings and beliefs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Attitudes to family are deeply rooted in the culture you grow up in.
example_sentences: People are deeply divided on whether tourism helps the island.
I was deeply impressed by how patient the volunteers were.

contexts.text: People are deeply divided on whether tourism helps the island.
I was deeply impressed by how patient the volunteers were.

confusables.difference: Deep is the adjective and also the adverb of physical depth: dig deep. Deeply is the adverb of feeling: care deeply.
Deeply collocates with a narrow set of words about emotion and belief. Very goes with almost any adjective, so do not swap them freely: deeply tired is wrong.

entry_json.avoid: Do not attach deeply to neutral adjectives. Deeply hot or deeply expensive is not English.

entry_json.definition: an occasion when somebody loses a game, an election or a battle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A narrow defeat in the final taught the team more than an easy win would have.
example_sentences: The party suffered a heavy defeat at the last election.
Learning to accept defeat is part of playing any sport.

contexts.text: The party suffered a heavy defeat at the last election.
A narrow defeat in the final taught the team more than an easy win would have.

confusables.difference: Loss is the neutral word and also covers losing money or people. Defeat is specifically being beaten by an opponent.
Failure means not achieving something; defeat means somebody else beat you.

entry_json.avoid: As a verb, defeat takes the loser as its object: "we defeated them", not "we defeated to them".

entry_json.definition: the act of protecting somebody or something from attack or criticism, or the means used to do so
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Spending on defence has risen while spending on schools has been frozen.
example_sentences: Vaccination is the body's first line of defence against infection.
He said nothing in his own defence, which surprised everyone.

contexts.text: Spending on defence has risen while spending on schools has been frozen.
He said nothing in his own defence, which surprised everyone.

confusables.difference: Defence is the British spelling and the one the examiner expects if you are writing British English; defense is American. Keep one variety throughout the paper.
Protection is general safety from harm. Defence implies an attack, or an argument being answered.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix British and American spellings in the same essay; defence and defense in one text looks careless.

entry_json.definition: to protect somebody or something from attack, or to give reasons in support of something that has been criticised
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The minister defended the decision by pointing to the cost of the alternative.
example_sentences: Sea walls defend the town against winter storms.
It is hard to defend a policy that has produced no measurable results.

contexts.text: It is hard to defend a policy that has produced no measurable results.
I had to defend my choice of course to almost everyone in the family.

confusables.difference: Protect is general prevention of harm, including from weather or accidents. Defend implies an attacker or a critic.
Support means you are in favour. Defend means you are answering an attack, so it presupposes criticism.

entry_json.avoid: Use defend something against or from something. "Defend to" is not English.

entry_json.definition: to say exactly what something means or what its limits are
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Before arguing about success, it is worth defining what the word means here.
example_sentences: The study defines a young worker as anyone under twenty-five.
Poverty is defined differently in different countries, which makes comparison hard.

contexts.text: Poverty is defined differently in different countries, which makes comparison hard.
It depends how you define a good job, really.

confusables.difference: Describe tells you what something is like. Define fixes its boundaries and states exactly what counts as an example of it.
Explain makes something understandable, often with reasons. Define only gives the meaning.

entry_json.avoid: The passive pattern is be defined as, not "be defined like".

entry_json.definition: certain and unlikely to change; clear and unambiguous
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a definite link between air quality and childhood asthma.
example_sentences: I cannot give you a definite answer until Friday.
The plan is not definite yet, so nothing has been booked.

contexts.text: There is a definite link between air quality and childhood asthma.
I cannot give you a definite answer until Friday.

confusables.difference: Definitive means final and authoritative: a definitive study nobody needs to repeat. Definite only means certain or clear.

entry_json.avoid: Watch the spelling: definite has an i in the middle, not an a. Definately is one of the most penalised misspellings in the exam.

entry_json.definition: a statement of exactly what a word means or what a thing is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Much of the disagreement comes from using two different definitions of poverty.
example_sentences: Look up the definition if you are not sure which sense is meant.
By any definition, this is a serious shortage of housing.

contexts.text: Much of the disagreement comes from using two different definitions of poverty.
Look up the definition if you are not sure which sense is meant.

confusables.difference: Meaning is what a word conveys. A definition is the formal statement of that meaning, usually written down.

entry_json.avoid: By definition means necessarily true from the meaning itself; do not use it as a filler for in my opinion.

entry_json.definition: a period of time when something happens later than planned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Long delays on the rail network push commuters back into their cars.
example_sentences: There was a two-hour delay because of the weather.
The project began without delay once the funding was approved.

contexts.text: Long delays on the rail network push commuters back into their cars.
There was a two-hour delay because of the weather.

confusables.difference: Postpone is a verb meaning to move an event to a later date on purpose. A delay is usually unplanned and measured in time lost.

entry_json.avoid: As a verb, delay takes the -ing form: "they delayed making a decision", not "delayed to make".

entry_json.definition: done on purpose rather than by accident
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The omission of cost figures from the report looks deliberate rather than careless.
example_sentences: It was a deliberate decision to keep the class sizes small.
Most of the damage was deliberate, according to the police.

contexts.text: The omission of cost figures from the report looks deliberate rather than careless.
It was a deliberate decision to keep the class sizes small.

confusables.difference: The two overlap closely. Deliberate is the commoner word and adds a hint of careful thought beforehand; intentional is more neutral and slightly more formal.
This is the direct opposite, and it is the contrast that gives deliberate its force in an argument.

entry_json.avoid: As a verb, deliberate is pronounced dɪˈlɪbəreɪt and means discuss carefully; do not mix the two pronunciations.

entry_json.definition: on purpose, with the result intended
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The timetable was deliberately designed so that nobody starts before nine.
example_sentences: He deliberately left his phone at home so that he could concentrate.
Prices were kept deliberately low to attract first-time customers.

contexts.text: Prices were kept deliberately low to attract first-time customers.
He deliberately left his phone at home so that he could concentrate.

confusables.difference: On purpose is the everyday spoken equivalent. Deliberately is the version to use in writing.
Carefully is about the manner of doing something; deliberately is about the intention behind it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use deliberately to mean slowly; that sense exists in literature but confuses examiners in an essay.

entry_json.definition: great pleasure, or something that gives great pleasure
entry_json.own_context_sentence: To my delight, the course turned out to be far more practical than I expected.
example_sentences: She watched her students' progress with obvious delight.
The garden is a delight in early summer.

contexts.text: To my delight, the course turned out to be far more practical than I expected.
The restored gardens are a delight for visitors of every age.

confusables.difference: Pleasure is the general word. Delight is stronger and shows on your face, so it fits sudden good news better than a quiet enjoyable evening.
Enjoyment lasts through an activity; delight is a burst of feeling, often at a surprise.

entry_json.avoid: Delight is too warm for Task 2 argument; keep it for Speaking and for descriptive writing.

entry_json.definition: very pleased
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was delighted when I heard that the scholarship had come through.
example_sentences: We would be delighted to have you stay with us.
My parents were delighted with the results, though I was not.

contexts.text: I was delighted when I heard that the scholarship had come through.
We would be delighted to welcome new members from the local area.

confusables.difference: Happy is the everyday word and can describe a lasting state. Delighted is stronger and reacts to a specific event, so "I am delighted with my life" sounds odd.
Pleased is calm approval; delighted is enthusiastic. In a formal letter, delighted is warmer and pleased is safer.

entry_json.avoid: Delighted is already extreme, so avoid "very delighted"; use absolutely delighted instead.

entry_json.definition: to take goods or letters to a place; or to provide what was promised
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Online shopping only works where parcels can be delivered reliably.
example_sentences: The supermarket delivers on the same day if you order before ten.
The scheme has not delivered the savings that were promised.

contexts.text: The scheme has not delivered the savings that were promised.
The supermarket delivers on the same day if you order before ten.

confusables.difference: You send something from where you are; the courier delivers it at the other end. The sender and the deliverer are rarely the same.
Provide simply makes something available. Deliver implies it reaches the person, and often that a promise is being kept.

entry_json.avoid: Deliver something to somebody, not "deliver somebody something" in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: the act of taking goods or letters to a place, or the goods taken
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Free delivery has done more to change shopping habits than any advertising campaign.
example_sentences: The delivery is due between two and four this afternoon.
Rising fuel costs have pushed up delivery charges for rural customers.

contexts.text: Rising fuel costs have pushed up delivery charges for rural customers.
The delivery is due between two and four this afternoon.

confusables.difference: Shipping is the American term for the same charge and also means transport by sea. In British English, delivery is the ordinary word for parcels.

entry_json.avoid: Delivery also means giving birth and the manner of giving a speech; make the context clear.

entry_json.definition: to say that something is not true; or to refuse to allow somebody to have something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Few people now deny that the climate is changing; the argument is about what to do.
example_sentences: The company denied that it had known about the fault.
Millions of children are still denied access to secondary education.

contexts.text: Millions of children are still denied access to secondary education.
He denied breaking it, but nobody else had been in the room.

confusables.difference: Refuse is saying no to a request. Deny is saying that a statement is false, or withholding something a person is entitled to.
Reject means turn down an offer or an idea. Deny an accusation means you claim it is untrue.

entry_json.avoid: Deny is followed by -ing or that, never by an infinitive: "he denied taking it", not "he denied to take it".

entry_json.definition: the act of leaving a place, especially at the start of a journey
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Check the departure board, because the platform often changes at the last minute.
example_sentences: Our departure was delayed by fog for almost three hours.
Departures from the main airport have doubled in ten years.

contexts.text: Departures from the main airport have doubled in ten years.
Check the departure board, because the platform often changes at the last minute.

confusables.difference: These are the paired opposites you see on every airport screen: departures leave, arrivals come in.
Leaving is the everyday gerund. Departure is the formal noun used on signs, timetables and in reports.

entry_json.avoid: Departure is formal. In conversation, "before we left" sounds far more natural than "before our departure".

entry_json.definition: very unhappy, often for a long time; or suffering from the illness of depression
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students who work alone for months on end often become depressed without noticing.
example_sentences: He felt depressed for weeks after losing his job.
Rates of depressed mood among teenagers have risen alongside social media use.

contexts.text: Students who work alone for months on end often become depressed without noticing.
He felt depressed for weeks after losing his job.

confusables.difference: Depressed is how the person feels; depressing is what causes the feeling. "The weather is depressing" and "I am depressed" are both right, but swapping them is not.
Sad is ordinary and short-lived. Depressed suggests a heavier state and, in medical use, a diagnosed illness.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use depressed casually for mild disappointment; in English it carries a clinical weight that upset or fed up does not.

entry_json.definition: making you feel unhappy and without hope
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The figures on youth unemployment make depressing reading.
example_sentences: It is depressing to see so many empty shops on the high street.
Grey tower blocks with no green space are a depressing environment for children.

contexts.text: The figures on youth unemployment make depressing reading.
It is depressing to see so many empty shops on the high street.

confusables.difference: Depressing describes the cause; depressed describes the person affected. A depressing film can leave you depressed.

entry_json.avoid: Never say "I am depressing" when you mean you feel low; that says you depress other people.

entry_json.definition: the distance from the top to the bottom of something; or the quality of being detailed and serious
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course covers a lot of ground but lacks depth in any single area.
example_sentences: At a depth of two hundred metres, almost no light remains.
The article examines the issue in some depth.

contexts.text: At a depth of two hundred metres, almost no light remains.
The course covers a lot of ground but lacks depth in any single area.

confusables.difference: Deep is the adjective, depth the noun. Say "the lake is deep" or "the depth of the lake", never "the deep of the lake".
Depth measures downward from the surface; height measures upward from the ground. The same wall can have both.

entry_json.avoid: The set phrase is in depth, with no article: "studied in depth", not "studied in the depth".

entry_json.definition: to have earned something by what you have done or what you are like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nurses deserve better pay for the hours they actually work.
example_sentences: After six months of revision, she deserved to pass.
This proposal deserves serious attention rather than an immediate dismissal.

contexts.text: This proposal deserves serious attention rather than an immediate dismissal.
After six months of revision, she deserved to pass.

confusables.difference: Earn is about actually receiving something, usually money, through work. Deserve is about being entitled to it, whether or not you get it.
Merit as a verb is formal and used mainly of ideas: "the point merits discussion". Deserve works for people too.

entry_json.avoid: Deserve is a stative verb, so avoid the continuous: not "she is deserving a rest".

entry_json.definition: a strong wish to have or do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The desire to own a home shapes how young people spend their entire twenties.
example_sentences: There is little desire among voters for another round of reform.
His desire to travel outweighed his fear of leaving home.

contexts.text: The desire to own a home shapes how young people spend their entire twenties.
I have no desire to live in a big city, to be honest.

confusables.difference: A wish can be idle and unlikely. A desire is strong and motivates action, which is why essays talk about the desire for change.
A need is something you cannot do without. A desire is something you strongly want, whether or not it is necessary.

entry_json.avoid: Desire followed by a noun of a person can suggest romantic or sexual meaning; in essays keep it to desire for change or desire to do something.

entry_json.definition: feeling or showing that you have little hope and are ready to do anything; or needing something very badly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Families in desperate need of housing are being placed in hotels for months.
example_sentences: By July I was desperate for a break from studying.
The situation in the camps is described as desperate.

contexts.text: Families in desperate need of housing are being placed in hotels for months.
By July I was desperate for a break from studying.

confusables.difference: Hopeless means there is no hope left, and is often used of a situation. Desperate describes the person's reaction, and it drives them to act.
Eager is positive keenness. Desperate for is much stronger and implies real distress or urgent need.

entry_json.avoid: "Desperate for" in casual speech can just mean very keen, but in Task 2 it reads as extreme, so use it only for genuine hardship.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something happens even though something else might have prevented it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Despite the rise in fuel prices, car use has barely fallen.
example_sentences: Despite living in the city for years, I still get lost.
The scheme went ahead despite strong local opposition.

contexts.text: Despite the rise in fuel prices, car use has barely fallen.
Despite living in the city for years, I still get lost.

confusables.difference: Although is a conjunction and takes a full clause: although prices rose. Despite is a preposition and takes a noun or -ing: despite the rise, despite rising.
These mean the same thing and behave identically. In spite of is three words; despite never takes of.

entry_json.avoid: Never write "despite of". If you need a clause, use despite the fact that, or switch to although.

entry_json.definition: containing many facts or particulars
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council published a detailed plan for the new transport network.
example_sentences: She gave a detailed account of what had happened that morning.
A more detailed study is needed before any conclusion can be drawn.

contexts.text: A more detailed study is needed before any conclusion can be drawn.
She gave a detailed account of what had happened that morning.

confusables.difference: Specific means exact and particular rather than general. Detailed means containing a lot of information. A specific example can still be short; a detailed one is long.
Length is not the same as detail; a long answer can be vague and a short one precise.

entry_json.avoid: The British stress is on the first syllable, DEE-tailed. Do not say "detailful".

entry_json.definition: to discover or notice something, especially something that is not easy to see or hear
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Modern scanners can detect the disease years before symptoms appear.
example_sentences: The software detects unusual spending and blocks the card.
No trace of the chemical was detected in the water supply.

contexts.text: Modern scanners can detect the disease years before symptoms appear.
My bank app detected a strange payment and stopped it straight away.

confusables.difference: Discover is finding something new to everyone, often for the first time in history. Detect is noticing something that was already there but hidden.
Notice is casual human observation. Detect suggests instruments, tests or careful searching.

entry_json.avoid: Detect is too technical for everyday speech: "I detected a nice smell" sounds strange where noticed or smelled would do.

entry_json.definition: to control or decide what something will be; or to find out something exactly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Family income still largely determines which university a student attends.
example_sentences: Researchers are trying to determine why the numbers fell so quickly.
The size of the grant determines how many places the college can offer.

contexts.text: Family income still largely determines which university a student attends.
The weather pretty much determines what we do at the weekend.

confusables.difference: Decide is a person choosing. Determine can be an impersonal factor causing a result: rainfall determines the harvest, but rainfall cannot decide anything.
Affect means to have some influence on. Determine is far stronger: it fixes the outcome.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use determine when you only mean influence; it overstates the claim and weakens an argument.

entry_json.definition: having decided firmly to do something and not letting anything stop you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She was determined to finish the degree while working nights.
example_sentences: He is a determined student who never misses a deadline.
The council seems determined to push the plan through regardless of objections.

contexts.text: She was determined to finish the degree while working nights.
The council seems determined to push the plan through regardless of objections.

confusables.difference: Both refuse to change, but determined is a compliment about persistence towards a goal, while stubborn criticises refusal to listen.
Confident is believing you will succeed; determined is refusing to stop trying, even without that belief.

entry_json.avoid: Determined is followed by to plus infinitive, not by -ing: "determined to succeed", not "determined succeeding".

entry_json.definition: the process of growing or becoming more advanced; or a new event or a new group of buildings
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Economic development has lifted millions out of poverty but strained the environment.
example_sentences: The early years are critical for a child's development.
A large housing development is planned on the edge of the town.

contexts.text: Economic development has lifted millions out of poverty but strained the environment.
A large housing development is planned on the edge of the town.

confusables.difference: Growth is getting bigger in size or number. Development is getting better or more advanced, and can happen without growth.
Progress is uncountable movement towards a goal. Development can be countable when it means a new event or a building project.

entry_json.avoid: Development is uncountable when it means the process; "the developments of the country" should be "the development of the country".

entry_json.definition: a simple drawing that explains how something works or shows the parts of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The diagram shows how rainwater is collected, filtered and stored.
example_sentences: A labelled diagram makes the process far easier to follow than a paragraph.
Draw a diagram if the explanation gets complicated.

contexts.text: The diagram shows how rainwater is collected, filtered and stored.
Draw a diagram if the explanation gets complicated.

confusables.difference: A graph plots numbers against axes. A diagram explains a structure or a process and usually has no numerical scale.
In Task 1, chart covers bar charts and pie charts, which show data. Diagram is the word for process and map questions.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 process questions, write "the diagram illustrates", not "the diagram tells us".

entry_json.definition: a clear, extremely hard precious stone; also a shape with four equal sides standing on a point
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Diamond mining has brought wealth to a few regions and conflict to others.
example_sentences: The ring has a small diamond set in silver.
Diamond is used in industry because nothing else cuts as cleanly.

contexts.text: Diamond mining has brought wealth to a few regions and conflict to others.
The ring has a small diamond set in silver.

confusables.difference: Crystal is any solid with a regular structure, and also a kind of high-quality glass. A diamond is one specific precious stone.

entry_json.avoid: The first syllable is DIE, not DEE. Note the silent second a in the spelling: d-i-a-m-o-n-d.

entry_json.definition: a problem, or the state of being hard to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many graduates have difficulty finding work in the field they trained for.
example_sentences: The main difficulty is that the two datasets were collected differently.
She had no difficulty in persuading the committee.

contexts.text: Many graduates have difficulty finding work in the field they trained for.
I had difficulty understanding the accent at first, but it got easier.

confusables.difference: A problem is a specific thing to be solved and is always countable. Difficulty is often uncountable and describes how hard something is.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is have difficulty doing something, not "have difficulty to do something".

entry_json.definition: to make a hole in the ground or move earth, usually with a tool or machine
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Workers had to dig a channel to carry the water away from the road.
example_sentences: We spent the morning digging the vegetable bed over.
Wells were dug by hand long before machinery arrived.

contexts.text: Wells were dug by hand long before machinery arrived.
We spent the morning digging the vegetable bed over.

confusables.difference: You drill a narrow hole with a rotating tool, in rock, wood or teeth. You dig in soft ground, usually with a spade or an excavator.

entry_json.avoid: Dig is irregular: dig, dug, dug. "Digged" is not a word.

entry_json.definition: in a straight line or without anything in between; or in an honest and clear way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rising fuel costs affect food prices directly, because everything has to be transported.
example_sentences: You can apply directly to the university rather than through an agency.
She answered the question directly instead of avoiding it.

contexts.text: Rising fuel costs affect food prices directly, because everything has to be transported.
You can apply directly to the university rather than through an agency.

confusables.difference: Direct is the adjective, and in a few phrases also an adverb, as in fly direct. Directly is the ordinary adverb and is safer in writing.
Directly can mean immediately in British English, but the main academic sense is without anything in between, so use immediately when you mean time.

entry_json.avoid: In an essay, keep directly for the without-an-intermediary sense; using it for at once can confuse the reader.

entry_json.definition: any substance that makes something unclean, such as mud or dust
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air filters have to be changed often because of the dirt in city air.
example_sentences: The windows had not been cleaned for months and were thick with dirt.
Wash your hands properly to remove dirt and bacteria.

contexts.text: Wash your hands properly to remove dirt and bacteria.
The windows had not been cleaned for months and were thick with dirt.

confusables.difference: Soil is earth that plants grow in and is a neutral, even positive word. Dirt is the same material once it is somewhere unwanted.
Dust is fine dry powder in the air or on surfaces; dirt is the general term and includes mud and grease.

entry_json.avoid: Dirt is uncountable: not "a dirt" or "many dirts".

entry_json.definition: something that makes a situation worse or less favourable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main disadvantage of working from home is that the day never really ends.
example_sentences: Every method has advantages and disadvantages worth weighing up.
Children from poorer families are at a clear disadvantage in this system.

contexts.text: Children from poorer families are at a clear disadvantage in this system.
The main disadvantage of working from home is that the day never really ends.

confusables.difference: A drawback is a specific unwanted feature of a plan or product. Disadvantage is broader and also describes an unfair position a person is in.

entry_json.avoid: The set phrase is at a disadvantage, not "in a disadvantage". Use disadvantage of doing something, not "disadvantage to do".

entry_json.definition: sad because something you hoped for did not happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was disappointed with my score, but I could see exactly where I lost marks.
example_sentences: Fans were disappointed that the concert was moved to another city.
She seemed disappointed in herself rather than angry with anyone else.

contexts.text: I was disappointed with my score, but I could see exactly where I lost marks.
Many residents were disappointed that the consultation changed nothing.

confusables.difference: Disappointed is the person; disappointing is the thing. "The film was disappointing, so I was disappointed".
Sad is general unhappiness. Disappointed always refers back to an expectation that was not met.

entry_json.avoid: Use disappointed with or in for people and things, and disappointed by for events. "Disappointed of" is wrong.

entry_json.definition: not as good as you hoped or expected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Attendance at the evening classes has been disappointing since the fee was introduced.
example_sentences: The results were disappointing given how much was invested.
It was a disappointing end to an otherwise excellent trip.

contexts.text: Attendance at the evening classes has been disappointing since the fee was introduced.
It was a disappointing end to an otherwise excellent trip.

confusables.difference: Disappointing describes the cause; disappointed describes the person who feels it.

entry_json.definition: a thin flat round object, especially one used for storing data or music
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most students have never owned a disc of any kind; everything is streamed.

The brakes work by pressing pads against a metal disc.

contexts.text: Most students have never owned a disc of any kind; everything is streamed.
Data storage moved from discs to remote servers within a single decade.

confusables.difference: British English prefers disc for physical round objects and disk for computer storage, as in hard disk. American English uses disk for both.

entry_json.definition: an amount of money taken off the usual price

contexts.text: Students get a discount on rail travel, which makes visiting home affordable.
Deep discounts late in the season attract buyers but cut profits.

entry_json.definition: not honest; intending to deceive people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Advertising that hides the real cost is not merely clever but dishonest.

entry_json.definition: to not like somebody or something

contexts.text: Most people dislike change at work even when it eventually benefits them.
I dislike crowded places, so I travel outside the rush hour.

confusables.difference: Hate is far stronger and more emotional. Dislike is measured, which makes it the better choice in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: to decide that something is not worth considering; or to officially remove somebody from a job

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is dismiss something as something: dismissed the plan as unrealistic, not "dismissed the plan to be unrealistic".

entry_json.definition: an arrangement of things for people to look at; or the screen that shows information
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The museum's display of local pottery draws more visitors than its paintings.

contexts.text: The museum's display of local pottery draws more visitors than its paintings.
The winning photographs are on display in the main hall.

confusables.difference: An exhibition is the whole organised event, often ticketed. A display is one arrangement of objects, which may be part of an exhibition.

entry_json.avoid: The fixed phrase is on display, with no article: not "on the display" when you mean shown to the public.

entry_json.definition: to give or spread things among a number of people or over an area
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Aid was distributed unevenly, so the remoter villages received almost nothing.

They distributed leaflets outside the station all morning.

confusables.difference: Share means several people use or have part of the same thing. Distribute means an organiser hands out portions to each person.

entry_json.definition: the way something is shared out or spread over an area, or the act of doing this

Distribution costs rise steeply once deliveries leave the main routes.

contexts.text: The map shows an uneven distribution of doctors between urban and rural areas.
The unequal distribution of wealth is at the centre of the debate.

confusables.difference: Division is splitting something into parts. Distribution is about where those parts end up or how they are spread.

entry_json.avoid: Distribution is normally uncountable here: "the distribution of income", not "the distributions of income".

entry_json.definition: an area of a town or country, especially one with a particular character or an official boundary
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The financial district empties completely at weekends.

contexts.text: The financial district empties completely at weekends.
She grew up in a quiet residential district near the river.

confusables.difference: Area is the general word for any space, large or small. District suggests a defined part of a town, often with an official boundary or a known character.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use district for a whole region or country; that is region or area.

entry_json.definition: to separate something into parts, or to cause people to disagree with each other

contexts.text: The issue divides opinion sharply even within the same generation.
The teacher divided the class into groups of four.

confusables.difference: Separate means to move things apart so they are no longer together. Divide means to break one thing into parts, which is why you divide a cake but separate two arguing children.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is divide something into parts, not "divide something in parts".

entry_json.definition: the act of separating something into parts; a disagreement between groups; or a section of a large organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The division of household work between men and women remains unequal in most countries.
example_sentences: Deep divisions within the party made agreement impossible.
She works in the research division of a pharmaceutical company.

contexts.text: The division of household work between men and women remains unequal in most countries.
She works in the research division of a pharmaceutical company.

confusables.difference: A department is usually smaller and functional, such as sales or HR. A division is a large self-contained part of a company, often with its own departments.

entry_json.avoid: In the disagreement sense, division is usually plural: deep divisions, not "a deep division", when several groups disagree.

entry_json.definition: a film or programme giving facts about a real subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A documentary about plastic in the oceans changed how our whole family shops.
example_sentences: I watched a documentary on migration that was better than any textbook.
Documentaries can shape public opinion faster than official reports.

contexts.text: A documentary about plastic in the oceans changed how our whole family shops.
Documentaries can shape public opinion faster than official reports.

confusables.difference: A film is usually a made-up story. A documentary presents real people and events, so calling one a film can mislead.

entry_json.avoid: Use documentary about or on a subject, not "documentary of".

entry_json.definition: connected with the home and family; or belonging to one country rather than to other countries
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Domestic energy use falls sharply once households can see what each appliance costs.
example_sentences: Domestic flights are cheaper but often just as polluting per passenger.
The share of domestic work done by men has risen slowly.

contexts.text: Domestic energy use falls sharply once households can see what each appliance costs.
Domestic flights are cheaper but often just as polluting per passenger.

confusables.difference: National means belonging to the nation as a whole, often with pride attached. Domestic contrasts with international, so domestic sales means sales inside the country.
Household is a noun used before another noun: household waste. Domestic is a true adjective and slightly more formal.

entry_json.avoid: Domestic animals means kept by people, not wild; it does not mean animals kept indoors.

entry_json.definition: to control or have the most important place in something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A handful of companies now dominate the market for online search.
example_sentences: The debate was dominated by questions about cost.
Tall glass towers dominate the skyline of the business district.

contexts.text: A handful of companies now dominate the market for online search.
Tall glass towers dominate the skyline of the business district.

confusables.difference: Control means directing something's behaviour. Dominate means being far larger or more powerful than everything else, which usually brings control with it.
Lead means being ahead, possibly by a little. Dominate implies the gap is overwhelming.

entry_json.avoid: Dominate takes a direct object: "they dominate the industry", not "they dominate over the industry".

entry_json.definition: to give money or goods to a person or organisation that needs help
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Supermarkets that donate unsold food waste far less than those that throw it away.
example_sentences: She donates a small amount to the food bank every month.
The land was donated to the city by a local family.

contexts.text: Supermarkets that donate unsold food waste far less than those that throw it away.
She donates a small amount to the food bank every month.

confusables.difference: Give works between any two people. Donate is for charities, hospitals and public institutions, and implies no payment in return.

entry_json.avoid: Donate something to an organisation, not "donate for". The noun is donation, not "donatement".

entry_json.definition: a feeling of being uncertain about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is little doubt that remote working is here to stay in some form.
example_sentences: Serious doubts remain about whether the target can be met.

contexts.text: Serious doubts remain about whether the target can be met.
I had my doubts at first, but the course turned out to be excellent.

confusables.difference: A question asks for information. A doubt is uncertainty about whether something is true, so you raise a question but you have a doubt.

entry_json.avoid: The b in doubt is silent. As a verb, doubt is followed by whether or if, not by that, in careful writing.

entry_json.definition: towards a lower place, level or amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The line moves downwards from 2015 onwards, reaching its lowest point in 2019.

contexts.text: The line moves downwards from 2015 onwards, reaching its lowest point in 2019.
The path slopes gently downwards towards the lake.

entry_json.definition: a group of twelve; in the plural, a large but vague number
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Dozens of small shops have closed since the retail park opened.

contexts.text: Dozens of small shops have closed since the retail park opened.
I bought a dozen eggs on the way home.

confusables.difference: Dozens of is a rough estimate in the tens; a lot of gives no scale at all. In Task 1 use the actual figures instead of either.

entry_json.avoid: After a number, dozen has no s: two dozen eggs. Only the vague plural takes both s and of: dozens of eggs.

entry_json.definition: an early version of a piece of writing that will be changed before it is finished
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My first draft was three hundred words too long, so most of the editing was cutting.

Nobody writes a good essay in one draft.

contexts.text: The committee is considering a draft of the new policy.
My first draft was three hundred words too long, so most of the editing was cutting.

confusables.difference: In British English, draught is the cold air coming under a door and the beer from a barrel; draft is the version of a document. The spelling separates two different words.
